analysis.one_liner: Adds a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates prices directly with drug makers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 54 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in two House committees until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a government-run prescription drug plan to Medicare's newly created Part D benefit, available nationwide. It required the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers — overriding the 2003 Medicare law's bar on federal price negotiation — and to steer the plan toward cheaper equivalents of brand-name drugs. The plan's premium would start at $35 a month in 2006, and seniors could choose it alongside private drug plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — tens of millions of seniors and disabled people — would gain a nationwide public drug plan with federally negotiated prices and a uniform $35 monthly premium in 2006, an alternative to private plans that bargain individually and cannot pool the buying power of the whole program. Taxpayers would also stand to benefit, since lower purchase prices would reduce the federal subsidy behind the drug benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Directs the HHS Secretary to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans with a service area covering the entire United States, giving beneficiaries in every region a public option alongside private plans.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers to cut the purchase price of covered Part D drugs and to encourage cheaper therapeutic equivalents, using strategies like those of other federal purchasers.
Explicitly overrides the section of the 2003 Medicare law that barred the government from interfering in drug price negotiations, lifting the 'non-negotiation' rule for the new public plan.

Sets the plan's premium uniformly nationwide at $35 a month for 2006, guarantees at least one $35 plan that year, and bases later-year premiums on the plan's actual average per-person cost including administration.
Allows the Secretary to designate the Medicare-operated plan as the 'fallback' plan in areas where private fallback plans are thin, giving beneficiaries there a guaranteed public choice.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the bill's direct cost through lower negotiated prices on drugs sold to the plan and pressure to substitute cheaper therapeutic equivalents. Private insurers selling Part D plans would face a nationwide government-run competitor, including the possibility of the public plan being designated the lower-cost fallback option in some areas. No broad new tax is specified; the plan's premium is set to cover its own costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Negotiated prices and a push toward therapeutic equivalents would cut what manufacturers collect on Medicare drugs; the standard good-faith objection is that lower drug revenue could reduce investment in developing new medicines.

The bill layered a national public plan on top of Part D's private-plan architecture rather than replacing it, creating two parallel systems to administer, and after 2006 the premium floats to the plan's actual average cost — so if negotiations underdelivered, beneficiaries' premiums would rise instead.

Because the Secretary could designate the Medicare plan as the fallback option where private coverage is unavailable, critics read the bill as a step toward a single government drug benefit, while supporters read the same clause as a coverage guarantee — a genuine design ambiguity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries, a nationwide public plan with federally negotiated prices and a $35 starting premium promised real savings on prescription drugs at a moment when the brand-new benefit barred the government from negotiating prices at all. The main costs fall on drug makers' Medicare revenue and on private Part D insurers facing competition, with a secondary, real tradeoff that less manufacturer revenue could slow development of new drugs. The design was incremental — private plans stayed in place — so the drawbacks are modest relative to the price relief offered, though the floating premium after 2006 left some uncertainty about how much beneficiaries would actually save.

outcome.mechanism: Two House committees sent it to their health subcommittee in February 2004, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the two-year Congress expired in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) introduced the bill on Feb. 4, 2004, joined as original cosponsors by 22 House Democrats including Jan Schakowsky, Henry Waxman, and John Conyers.
The House referred it the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two panels with jurisdiction over the Medicare drug benefit.
In February 2004 both committees referred the bill to their Health Subcommittee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote after that.
The bill would have amended the Part D drug benefit created by the 2003 Medicare law, directing the HHS Secretary to offer one or more Medicare-operated drug plans available nationwide.

It required the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce purchase prices and to encourage cheaper therapeutic equivalents, expressly overriding the 2003 law's section barring the government from interfering in drug price negotiations.
The Medicare-operated plan's premium would be $35 a month in 2006, uniform nationwide, and the Secretary had to ensure at least one plan at that price.
The cosponsor list grew to 54, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, brand-name drug manufacturers kept the 2003 law's structure — the government barred from negotiating prices — and private insurers kept Part D as a market of subsidized private plans with no public competitor. Medicare beneficiaries continued to pay prices set through private-plan bargaining rather than federal negotiation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, while Republicans held the House majority and both committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill.

industries.note: The bill required HHS to negotiate purchase prices directly and to steer the plan toward cheaper therapeutic equivalents, reversing the 2003 law's provision keeping the government out of price talks. Drug makers' Medicare pricing power was the bill's principal target.

industries.industry: Private health insurers selling Part D plans
industries.note: A Medicare-operated plan would compete nationwide with the private plans that the new drug benefit routes federal subsidies through, and could even be designated the cheaper fallback plan where private coverage is thin. The bill left the private-plan structure in place but gave seniors a public alternative to it.
